claims.text: Local lattice distortion is the dominant mechanism governing strength and deformation in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Atomic size misfit produces local lattice distortions in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Chemical disorder produces local lattice distortions in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Local lattice distortions hinder dislocation motion.
Local lattice distortions increase the energy barriers for dislocation glide.
Increased barriers to dislocation glide result in higher yield strength.
Samples with greater measured local lattice distortion will have higher yield strength than lower-distortion baseline samples.
Samples with greater measured local lattice distortion will exhibit enhanced strain hardening relative to lower-distortion baseline samples.
Greater local lattice distortion may alter failure modes relative to lower-distortion baseline samples.
The proposed mechanism should govern behavior at ambient temperature and typical tensile or compression strain rates when samples have comparable, predominantly single-phase microstructures.
The governing effects may differ in alloys containing significant secondary phases.
The governing effects may differ at very high strain rates or temperatures.
Pair-distribution-function analysis or diffuse scattering can quantify differences in local lattice distortion.
Short-range order or local chemical clustering may also contribute to mechanical behavior.

A lack of statistically significant association between distortion and the specified mechanical outcomes, or equal or better performance by lower-distortion samples, is proposed as a falsifying result.
